bibliography.checked_against: the article's first page (citation line) and Crossref
bibliography.note: Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 49: 2605–2610, 1992 (issue 12 per Crossref); authors Susan Watson, Edward McCauley, John A. Downing

claims.claim: small edible algae 'do not vary systematically with phosphorus' across north-temperate lakes, while the inedible fraction does
claims.source_value: true of the authors' compilation — 101 lake observations with size-fraction data, from published studies (67 sources, 362 lakes in all), mean summer epilimnetic values, TP 1–200 µg/L, edible = cells or colonies < 35–50 µm (Utermöhl biovolume as wet mass) — but the source never says 'north-temperate': the lakes' geography is not given. Inedible biomass rose > 40-fold and sigmoidally; edible 'appears to increase slightly and then levels off' between ~5 and 30 µg TP/L
claims.location: p. 2605 (PDF p. 1), abstract; p. 2606 (PDF p. 2), Data and Analyses; p. 2607 (PDF p. 3), Results; p. 2608 (PDF p. 4), Table 1
claims.quote: inedible algal biomass increases nonlinearly with TP by more than 40-fold
claims.conditions: Table 1: edible biomass n = 101, cubic regression on log TP r² = 0.22 (P < 0.0001); inedible n = 101, r² = 0.44, LOWESS sigmoidal; TP range 1–200 µg/L for both
claims.note: The quoted phrase is the abstract's, and the Results repeat it ('Edible algae, on the other hand, do not vary systematically with TP'), so the quote stands; drop 'north-temperate' (or say 'across 101 lakes compiled from the literature') and the '(abstract only)' tag. Note that the authors' own parametric fit for edible algae is significant though weak (r² 0.22), so 'not systematically' is their reading of a flat-ish, noisy relation.

claims.quote: do not vary systematically with phosphorus
claims.note: As the authors conclude; the slight rise and levelling between ~5 and 30 µg TP/L and the weak significant cubic fit (r² 0.22) are the fine print.

notes: Most useful for Hot Brook (TP 5–25 µg/L): the community-structure thresholds (p. 2608, Fig. 5): below ~8–10 µg TP/L total biomass is dominated by edible algae; above that is a transition zone where edible and inedible are similar in relative abundance but the inedible fraction changes faster; above ~30 µg/L inedible algae rapidly dominate, and above ~50 µg/L biomass is almost entirely the large fraction. Total algal biomass (biovolume) is sigmoid in TP: little change below 5 µg/L, a roughly constant rate of rise from ~6 to 60 µg/L, slowing above 65–75 µg/L (LOWESS). The project's NLA classification of 'edible' is taxonomic (flagellates, small diatoms, non-filamentous greens), Watson's is by size (< 35–50 µm), so the two are not strictly comparable.
